summary: Describes problems of receiving DHCPv6 messages of an unknown type and defines how servers, clients, and relay agents should behave. It updates RFC 3315 and was replaced by RFC 8415.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes a computer gets a message it does not know. This tells it what to do instead of getting confused. It has since been replaced.

questions: how to handle unknown dhcpv6 messages
how should relay agents handle unknown dhcpv6 messages
what happens when a server receives an unknown dhcpv6 message type
how does forward compatibility work in dhcpv6
can old relay agents forward new dhcpv6 message types
subtitle: Defines how DHCPv6 nodes should handle messages with unknown types

tldr.problem: RFC 3315 does not specify what DHCPv6 servers, clients, and relay agents should do when they receive a message with a type they do not recognize. This can cause inconsistent behavior and break forward compatibility with new message types.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7283 defines clear rules: relay agents forward unknown messages toward servers (following normal forwarding rules), while servers and clients silently discard unknown messages. This allows new DHCPv6 message types to work with old relay agents.
tldr.outcome: DHCPv6 can now be extended with new message types in the future, and old relay agents will automatically forward them correctly without needing updates.

today: RFC 7283 is a Proposed Standard that updated DHCPv6 message handling for forward compatibility. It has been obsoleted by RFC 8415, which consolidated the DHCPv6 specification.

sections.title: The Problem of Unknown Messages
sections.content:
DHCPv6 is a protocol for configuring IPv6 hosts with network information and addresses. Like any protocol, DHCPv6 may be extended with new message types in the future. However, RFC 3315 does not specify how servers, clients, and relay agents should behave when they encounter a message type they do not recognize.

This lack of specification creates problems. Relay agents may drop unknown messages without forwarding them, preventing new message types from reaching their intended recipients. Servers or clients might try to process messages they do not understand, leading to unpredictable behavior. This makes it difficult to deploy new DHCPv6 features if older devices are in the network path.
sections.plainLanguage: When a computer gets a message for a feature it doesn't know about, nobody knows what to do. This says what each type of computer should do so the message can get where it needs to go.

sections.title: Design Principle: Forward Compatibility
sections.content:
RFC 7283 solves this by applying a simple forward-compatibility principle: unknown messages should be treated as if they are valid messages, allowing them to pass through the network correctly. This ensures that when new DHCPv6 message types are defined in future RFCs, they will work automatically with older relay agents that were manufactured before those new messages were defined.

The key insight is that a relay agent's job is to forward messages, not to validate them. By relaying unknown messages the same way it would relay known messages, a relay agent future-proofs the protocol. Servers and clients, on the other hand, can safely discard messages they do not understand without risk, since messages that servers and clients do not expect to receive are dropped anyway.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is simple: a relay's job is just to pass messages along, so it should pass along things it doesn't understand too. A server or client can throw away messages it doesn't understand because nobody sent them those messages anyway.

sections.title: What Relay Agents Must Do
sections.content:
A relay agent's behavior is defined by the message type it receives. A Relay-reply message is always sent toward the client, following the path defined in the message. All other message types, including unknown types, are sent toward the server following the relay agent's default forwarding path.

RFC 7283 specifies that a message is valid for relaying if it is a Relay-forward message, if the relay recognizes it and is not the intended target, or if the relay does not recognize the message type. By including the third case, the specification ensures that unknown message types will be forwarded toward the server, allowing new DHCPv6 applications to reach servers even when relay agents have not been updated to recognize them.
sections.plainLanguage: A relay looks at the message type. If it is a Relay-reply, send it to the client. Everything else, including messages the relay has never seen, goes toward the server. This way new messages automatically get forwarded right.

sections.title: What Clients and Servers Must Do
sections.content:
A DHCPv6 client or server MUST silently discard any received message with an unknown message type. This simple rule means that if a client or server receives a message it does not recognize, it simply ignores it without error reporting or further processing.

This behavior is safe because clients and servers do not expect to receive unknown message types in normal operation. A server that receives an unknown message type on the wire was not expecting that message anyway, so discarding it causes no harm. Similarly, a client discards unexpected messages. This clean, simple rule allows servers and clients to be unmodified when new DHCPv6 message types are defined, since they will simply discard the new types if they do not understand them.
sections.plainLanguage: If you are a server or a client and you get a message you don't know, just throw it away. Don't try to understand it or tell anyone about it.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
The changes defined in RFC 7283 create no fundamentally new security issues beyond those already present in RFC 3315. However, because relay agents now forward all unknown message types, a malicious attacker could send crafted DHCPv6 messages with arbitrary type codes to interfere with the relaying function. This is already possible using known message type codes, so the new capability does not significantly increase risk.

The main recommendation is that relay agents, clients, and servers be updated to follow this specification. However, in most deployments, directly attacking a client on the local network is easier than exploiting relayed messages. Additionally, administrators can configure relay agents with firewall rules to drop specific message types if needed. The specification itself does not prevent such administrative controls.
sections.plainLanguage: A bad person could try to fool a relay by sending fake messages. But they can already do that with real message types, so this doesn't create new problems. Network managers can add rules to block messages if they want.
